source: Li, Li, Yang, Ma, Su (2026) Learning to Disprove: Formal Counterexample Generation with LLMs
finding: Trains an LLM to propose a counterexample and prove it in Lean 4. Data come from dropping one hypothesis of a provable theorem and negating the claim. A second reward checks that the dropped hypothesis is false for the candidate, so training gets signal even when the main proof fails.
numbers: About 575K (575,039) candidate counterexample problems from 212,463 source items. CounterMath is described as only 1,216 problems. Claimed pass@1 gain of 47% to 74% relative to the strongest baseline. Validation pass@1/4/9: 49.8/52.7/54.1% vs best baseline 25.4/36.0/39.9% (Leanabell).
quote: Counterexample training: drop hypothesis, negate conjecture, prove both.
limits: Lean-formal counterexamples only; the page header says rejected from ICLR 2026; the authors report counts, not rates, because the existing benchmark has inaccuracies.
agent_relevance: Counterexample search can be a checkable step with a formal verifier. The two-part check (is the example valid, and which assumption does it break) is a typed reaction to a counterexample, close to Lakatos exception-barring. Only indirect evidence for GAP 1: it trains, it does not compare typed and untyped retry.

source: Li et al. (2026) Learning to Disprove, Table 2 benchmarks
finding: On three new benchmarks the tuned model solves more problems than general LLMs and open provers at pass@1, 4 and 9. At pass@1 it solves 95, 69 and 63 more problems than the strongest baseline.
numbers: FOR-COUNTER, VERI-REASON, VERI-FORMALIZE. Tuned model solves 222/213/174 at pass@1 per the PDF table vs best baseline 127/144/111. Relative gains 74%, 47%, 56%. VERI-FORMALIZE and VERI-REASON are 3K problems each.
limits: Table text was garbled in PDF extraction; relative-gain labels may be misaligned, so treat the per-column numbers as approximate. Test sets built by the same pipeline as training data.
agent_relevance: Verifying reasoning steps and autoformalised statements by counterexample search works as a filter. Supports funnel design (K01) but only inside Lean.

source: CRAFT authors (2026) Counterexample-guided Repair And Falsification of Theorems in ML and Optimization (ICML 2026 page)
finding: An LLM labels a claim true, false or uncertain. A code verifier searches for counterexamples and feeds them back. The claim is repaired and re-checked. This is a counterexample-then-repair loop.
numbers: 50 claims across 25 ML/optimization families; 7 models. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct accuracy 78% to 94% with verifier feedback; all 25 canonical repair targets pass re-check. Feedback improved or kept accuracy for all seven models.
limits: Abstract page only, not the full paper. Tiny benchmark. Baseline is the round-1 LLM judgment, not an untyped retry at equal tokens. Search quality limits verifier reliability.
agent_relevance: Closest 2026 result to a measured counterexample-repair loop (GAP 1). It shows feedback helps. It does not show typing the reaction beats plain retry.

source: Martin and Pease (2013) Mathematical practice, crowdsourcing, and social machines
finding: Reads Lakatos's six methods (surrender, monster-barring, exception-barring, monster-adjusting, lemma-incorporation, proofs and refutations) and looks for them in MathOverflow and a mini-polymath thread. Names Pease's HRL as a computational representation of Lakatos and Colton's HR as theory formation by production rules.
numbers: In the sampled MathOverflow responses: errors found and corrected in 37%; explicit examples or counterexamples in 34%; citations in 56%. Monster-adjusting seen in the mini-polymath study.
quote: Where errors are spotted, either by the person who made them or by others, the style is to politely accept and correct them
limits: Descriptive coding of human threads. No outcome measure and no comparison of strategies. HRL is cited from Pease's thesis, but no benchmark numbers are given. So GAP 9 is not closed here.
agent_relevance: Gives a human base rate for counterexample use in live proof work. Not a test of the methods.

source: Martin and Pease (2013) Lakatos moves as triggers
finding: Most of Lakatos's moves are triggered by a counterexample. Monster-barring and monster-adjusting work on vague concept definitions. Exception-barring strengthens the conjecture by adding a condition. The paper notes Lakatos does not say how hidden assumptions arise.
numbers: Picture-frame polyhedron with V-E+F = 16-32+16 = 0 is the standard monster-barring example.
quote: Most of these are triggered by counterexamples
limits: Review of a philosophical account. No effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Gives the typology for a typed counterexample reaction: change the claim (exception-barring), change the definition (monster-barring), change a step (lemma-incorporation). Still untested in LLMs, so GAP 1 stays open.

source: Chen (2026) Lectures on AI for Mathematics
finding: A 159-page lecture text with a chapter on AI constructing counterexamples (RL in graph theory; LLM agents). Describes AI as doing exploration and conjecture and Lean as doing verification.
numbers: Chapter 5 'AI for Constructing Counterexamples' starts at p. 103; section 5.4 covers LLM agents. No new measured results extracted.
quote: AI is responsible for exploration and conjecture, while Lean is responsible for verification
limits: Only the table of contents, introduction and a few passages were read by text search. Secondary survey. A search summary said it describes a generator-verifier-revise loop, but I did not find that in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Survey support only. Do not cite for numbers.

source: Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner (2025) Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale: checker gaming
finding: The authors report a cheating phenomenon: the search found loopholes in the problem set-up rather than real solutions.
numbers: Two forms named: a leaky verifier when a global constraint such as positivity is replaced by a discrete check, and unreliable queries to cheap LLMs. No rate of occurrence is given.
quote: exploit artifacts (leaky verifier when approximating global constraints such as positivity by discrete versions of them
limits: Anecdotal. No count of events and no hold-out experiment. GAP 7 stays open for rates.
agent_relevance: Any code-checked claim loop needs a checker the generator cannot exploit. Add a hold-out or finer check and measure it.

source: Georgiev et al. (2025) Worked case: irregular function exploits numerical integration
finding: In one problem the authors let AlphaEvolve propose arbitrary functions instead of bounded step functions with fixed step sizes. It always eventually produced a highly irregular function that exploited the numerical integration in the scorer and got impossibly high scores. Restricting to bounded step functions fixed it and improved all earlier bounds in that section.
numbers: Qualitative: 'impossibly high scores'. No count of runs.
limits: One problem. No ablation with numbers.
agent_relevance: The fix was to shrink the hypothesis space so the checker is valid, not to add a second check. A design rule for checker guards.

source: Georgiev et al. (2025) Scope of the 67-problem study
finding: The authors took 67 problems, most turned into upper or lower bound searches. AlphaEvolve often matched known bounds, sometimes improved them, and sometimes did not match them. It finds constructions, not proofs of bounds. Prompting skill and scoring function design mattered.
numbers: 67 problems. Counts of matched, improved and failed problems were not extracted in this pass.
quote: Many of these quantities could be expressed as a supremum or infimum of some score function
limits: Counts still missing, so an 'improved on N of 67' figure is not verified. Authors note some gains could be matched by traditional methods.
agent_relevance: Constructions with a numeric score are the checkable niche. Open-ended conjecture refinement lacks such a score.

source: Aggarwal, Kim, Ek, Mishra (2026) Discovering mathematical concepts through a multi-agent system
finding: Two RL agents. A Conjecturing agent proposes statements. A Skeptical agent re-weights data points to make them hard to prove. Ablations: conjecturer only; full system; full with noisy provability; both agents without provability reward; conjecturer plus provability without skeptic.
numbers: Task is recovering the homology idea (two definitions of the Euler characteristic) from polyhedral data plus linear algebra. Runs on a laptop. The conjecturer-only control runs 50 steps per episode.
quote: central claim is that it is the nature of this interaction that is most important
limits: I opened the HTML but did not extract the result tables, so the size of the skeptic gain is not recorded here. A small symbolic RL system, not an LLM.
agent_relevance: GAP 10: still one domain, one task, one group. No replication found. Treat the skeptic gain (c01) as single-source.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2026) Limits stated by the authors
finding: The authors say rediscovery holds only within certain limits and that interestingness may not be formulable as an objective beyond restricted cases.
numbers: Single benchmark: Euler characteristic and homology from polyhedral data.
quote: All machine learning needs objectives to optimise.
limits: Self-reported limits. No external replication or other domain.
agent_relevance: Do not generalise the skeptic gain to LLM agents on open-ended math.

source: An, Ye, Pan, Zhang (2026) QED: open-source multi-agent system for proofs on open problems
finding: Planner, prover and separate verifier agents, run on frontier coding agents (Codex GPT-5.5 and others). Seven failure modes of single-query proving are named, each tied to a design fix: shared context, citation hallucination, effort misallocation, unstable plans, unfocused verification, problem modification, single-model bottleneck.
numbers: 18 expert-proposed research projects from 7 domain experts. 5 gave original complete proofs, confirmed by experts; 3 judged comparable to specialist-journal work. Cost about 100 to about 600 US dollars per case.
quote: Prover and verifier share context, producing circular reasoning
limits: Self-reported by the system authors. Experts were collaborators. No equal-token single-call baseline. Preprint v4, June 2026.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to GAP 5: a 2026 scaffold solved 5 of 18 open items. There is no matched no-scaffold arm.

source: An et al. (2026) QED verifier false-positive check
finding: Of 214 proof candidates from the prover and checked by the verifier, 17 were accepted. All 17 were accepted by the experts, so 0 false positives out of 17.
numbers: 214 candidates, 17 accepted, 0/17 false positives. False negatives not stated in the text I read.
limits: Only 17 accepted, so the upper bound on the false-positive rate is wide (about 18% at 95% by the rule of three). The text says earlier configurations gave more false positives.
agent_relevance: A separate verifier context looks like a useful guard against self-confirmation. The rate is not tight.

source: An et al. (2026) QED targeted ablations
finding: The authors ran qualitative ablations on two cases only, removing components, and say they are diagnostic and not estimates of success rate.
quote: These ablations are limited to two cases and are diagnostic
agent_relevance: Separating planning from execution is supported only by anecdote.

source: Sivakumar, Borchert, Cardenas, Lampouras (2025) Conjecturing: an overlooked step in formal mathematical reasoning (ConjectureBench)
finding: When the answer or bound is hidden ('unseen'), autoformalisation looks much worse than when the gold conjecture is in the problem. LEAN-FIRE, which interleaves informal reasoning with Lean, raises conjecture accuracy.
numbers: ConJudge for GPT-4.1 with LEAN-FIRE: seen 78.77 at pass@1 and 98.03 at pass@10; unseen without few-shot 26.70 and 61.27. DeepSeek-V3.1: seen 92.78 and 98.47; unseen 55.80 and 85.34. Average 23.7% drop from seen to unseen. LEAN-FIRE gives 13 new PutnamBench autoformalisations with GPT-4.1 and 7 with DeepSeek-V3.1. Conjecture gain on ConJudge averages 29.1% for GPT-4.1 and 14.0% for DeepSeek-V3.1.
quote: autoformalisation performance is substantially overestimated when the conjecture is accounted for
limits: ConJudge is an LLM grader tuned on human annotation. BEq+ is strict and may give false negatives. Gain in end-to-end formalisation was modest, and pass@10 slightly fell in one comparison.
agent_relevance: Conjecture-making is a separate step that drives results. Hiding the answer exposes the real difficulty. Supports a distinct conjecture state in the schema.

finding: Problems whose answer is embedded in the statement were rewritten into forms needing a numerical or expression answer, for example 'prove at least' became 'what is the minimum'.
numbers: The type table lists shares such as algebraic 39.0%, 36.1% and 24.9%.
limits: Table layout was garbled and category names were only partly recovered.

finding: A multi-agent sprint on ten research-level problems with adversarial verification and repair. The outcome is mixed and reported by ledger: problems 1, 2, 3, 8 closed with full validation; 5 and 7 closed with partial QC; 4 and 6 partial; 9 computational evidence only; 10 conditional.
numbers: 10 problems: 4 closed and validated, 2 closed with partial QC, 2 partial, 1 computational only, 1 conditional. Run Feb 11-13, 2026.
quote: structure-aware verification and layer-switching strategies improve reliability and calibration
limits: Single author, self-reported status, not peer reviewed. 'Closed' depends on its own QC. I read the abstract and parts of the text.
agent_relevance: The status vocabulary (closed, partial, conditional), which separates math status from validation status, is a useful output format for schema states. Not a controlled comparison.

source: Gap search note: Lakatos-typed reaction vs untyped retry (CounterMATH line of work)
finding: A web search, plus tries on arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar, found no study that compares typed Lakatos-style reactions with untyped retry. Nearest are CRAFT (d03), Learning to Disprove (d01) and CounterMATH.
numbers: Zero direct studies found. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429 and the arXiv API returned empty results; only one web search succeeded before the shared budget ran out.
limits: A negative result from a rate-limited search, so absence is weak evidence. The CounterMATH paper was not re-opened this session.
agent_relevance: GAP 1 stays open. Run it as our own test.
